summary: Corn growers must decide when to plant, how to use water and whether to rotate before the season is known, and a shifting climate makes that bet harder every year. We built Data Corn, an open-source web tool that turns 25 years of hindsight into this year's decision. A farmer outlines a field on a 3D globe with NASA satellite layers and an El Niño indicator. Data Corn replays the real daily weather of 2001 to 2025 from NASA POWER through a soil-water model on the field's USDA soil, showing when to plant, where water ran short and heat struck at silking, and how much irrigation was needed. During the season, NASA MODIS vegetation data tracks the field's green-up. For the Field Shift challenge, it compares three rotations side by side (corn after corn; corn and soybean; corn and soybean with rye cover), each with its evidence, unknowns and local risks, and marks the one matching the field's recent crops. One plain-English screen serves a farm manager and an agronomist: a season film with good harvests in similar years and days of water left, season stripes marking El Niño and La Niña years, decision cards, a PDF report and an optional AI assistant. No login. Why it matters: rotation adds about 0.96 t/ha to Midwest corn, yet warming could cut that benefit 7 to 17% by 2051-2070 (Zhou et al., 2024). Its results are scenarios from past climate, not forecasts, and support the farmer's judgment rather than replace local advice.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Data Corn shows a US corn producer how one field would have behaved in each of 25 past seasons, 2001 to 2025. You fly over a 3D globe with NASA layers, including clouds, rain and sea temperature now (GOES and GPM IMERG through NASA GIBS, and GHRSST MUR) and an El Niño indicator from NOAA's index, outline your field on the map and check a few prefilled details: season, planting date, hybrid maturity, irrigation and tillage. For that spot, the engine reads daily weather from NASA POWER and soil from the USDA soil survey (SSURGO). It computes reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation and runs a daily root-zone water balance. Crop stages follow growing degree days, and relative yield follows the FAO-33 seasonal response of maize to water. Each scenario is this season's observed days, if any, followed by one past season for the rest. One screen then shows a season film of the field's soil water over the map, with daily rain and irrigation, the range of the 25 seasons, the yield lost so far (FAO-33) and the key moments, and season stripes with El Niño and La Niña years marked from NOAA's index. Two numbers follow the film: "Good harvests in similar years", the share of past seasons that looked the same on that day (soil water and yield so far) and ended with less than 15 % loss from water; and a water battery, the days the field would last without rain or irrigation before stress, at the last 10 days' use. Over a US field the map shows a 1 m aerial photo (USDA NAIP, from USGS The National Map). The cards cover planting date (during a season, field progress from NASA MODIS NDVI takes its place), water and heat at silking, hybrid and frost, irrigation, waterlogging and rotation (the crop grown each year, from the USDA Cropland Data Layer). A panel, "Three ways to rotate", explains three strategies: corn after corn; corn and soybean, taking turns; and corn and soybean, with a rye cover crop. For the first two it rates the erosion risk from crop residue, slope and tillage. [#128] The engine also gives those two a relative erosion index from 0 to 100, based on Missouri plot measurements (Alberts et al. 1985); the rye option has no source yet, so it shows no data, and the example report has not been regenerated with the index. A PDF report downloads from the same screen. An optional SI assistant, labelled as such, answers questions about the example report's numbers; it reads them from the report and computes nothing.

What benefits does it have?

A producer sees the range of real seasons on their own field, instead of one average year that never happens. Two plain numbers follow the film, good harvests in similar years and the days of water left, so the state of the season reads at a glance. The screen is in plain English and US units, so a farm manager and an agronomist can read it together, and the cards say what to check in the field. [#127] A Help tab shows how each result is calculated, with the equations. A Display menu offers larger text, high contrast for sunlight and a calm mode without autoplay. The risk colours are safe for colour-blind readers, and a word and an icon always carry the meaning. Each rotation strategy lists why it is shown, its evidence and source, the benefits, what we do not know and the risks to check locally. It runs in a browser, with no login and no account.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We want producers to weigh planting, hybrid, irrigation and rotation choices before the season, with the range of past outcomes in view. On the High Plains, irrigation draws on the Ogallala aquifer, which NASA Earth Observatory describes as under stress. It reports that about 30 percent of the water once stored beneath Kansas was gone by 2018, and that about 40 percent more could go within 50 years if trends continue. Knowing in advance how much water a field would have needed in dry seasons helps plan that use. The tool supports the producer's judgment and the local agronomist's advice. It does not replace them.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Python 3.12 with FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy and SciPy for the engine, in layers (Clean Architecture) that keep the science apart from the data sources. TypeScript with Astro, React and MapLibre GL JS for the web app, and @react-pdf/renderer for the PDF report. GitHub Actions runs the checks on every pull request: ruff and more than 170 engine tests (pytest), then the web build, the type check and more than 180 unit tests (Vitest). Playwright smoke tests are run by hand. No special hardware. Claude Code and Codex helped write code, tests and documents, and Codex generated the line icons on our slides, which carry an SI-generated label. Every data source and method, with its licence, is in docs/REFERENCES.md in the repository.

How is your project creative?

It turns 25 years of daily weather into a film of one field's season, with season stripes you can tap to replay any year. Two readouts borrow from other fields: a good-harvests-in-similar-years line like the win probability in a sports broadcast, and a water battery like an electric car's range. The globe opens on the world now: clouds, rain and the El Niño warming of the Pacific. It puts rotation strategies side by side with what we do not know about each, not only their benefits. Decision tools for US corn already exist. DAWN, described in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society (2024), turns seasonal forecasts and crop models into planting, irrigation and fertilizer comparisons for Corn Belt farmers, with user accounts and a network of extension partners. Agroptimizer recommends corn and soybean management, and a 2024 study compared it with local experts in Wisconsin. Ours takes another route. It replays observed past seasons through a water balance on the soil of one drawn field, needs no login, and states what it does not know next to each rotation strategy. It gives scenarios from past climate, not forecasts, and it has no nutrient or profit model. We reviewed public information only, so another product may cover part of this.

What factors did your team consider?

Results are scenarios built from past climate, not forecasts. The good-harvests readout only counts past seasons that looked the same; it is not a forecast. The water battery assumes the last 10 days' use goes on. The 1 m aerial photo covers the continental US only; elsewhere the map keeps Sentinel-2. Weather comes from a grid about 50 km wide and soil from a survey, not from a probe in the field. Yield numbers come from published water-balance methods and are not calibrated against any farm's yields. Crop parameters are generic, and the degree days to maturity for each hybrid are not checked against a source yet. The rotation evidence comes mostly from Iowa studies, not from the High Plains. The model does not carry water between crops or model the water a rye cover uses. A card with no data says "No data" instead of showing a number. Where the soil survey has no soil or slope for a spot, the engine uses generic values and lists them in the report's data sources, as the About panel says. We do not know a producer's priorities, budget or risk tolerance, and the tool has not been tested with farmers or extension specialists yet. The app needs no login and asks for no personal data, and NASA appears only as a data source. No data server is deployed behind the public demo, so it shows real reports, computed in advance, for one example field in Nebraska under its four irrigation options, and invented sample numbers, labelled as such, for any other field or changed value.
